FrMS88-de3571-d1e111.summary: Poses the eighth question — whether a concept common to the simply simple and the primarily diverse can be abstracted — and, without preliminary arguments, answers no, understood of a quidditative concept. Distinguishes four kinds of concept that may nonetheless be common: of second intentions, of the most common attributes, of transcendental habitudes, and of privations.
claims: No common quidditative concept can be abstracted from simply simple and primarily diverse concepts.
There are four kinds of non-quidditative common concepts.

FrMS88-de3571-d1e133.summary: Example of the first kind: as the species is abstracted from Peter and Martin, so 'ultimate difference' is abstracted from ultimate differences and 'individual property' from individual properties, and predicated of them univocally.
claims: Second-intention concepts like 'ultimate difference' are univocally predicated of ultimate differences.

FrMS88-de3571-d1e144.summary: Example of the second kind: all ultimate differences are intelligible and volitable, hence true and good; truth and goodness are thus predicated univocally of all.
claims: Truth and goodness are predicated univocally of all ultimate differences.

FrMS88-de3571-d1e151.summary: Example of the third kind: transcendental relations encompassing all things, such as identity, diversity, and distinction, are predicated even of ultimate differences.
claims: Identity, diversity, and distinction are transcendental relations predicated of ultimate differences.

FrMS88-de3571-d1e159.summary: Example of the fourth kind: unity and simplicity, which seem to import privations, are predicated univocally of many primarily diverse items.
claims: Unity and simplicity, as privations, are predicated univocally of the primarily diverse.

FrMS88-de3571-d1e166.summary: Raises a difficulty: when an attribute belongs to many it seems to do so through a common notion; if these attributes belong to primarily diverse items, they would do so through a common notion, and the items would not be primarily diverse.
claims: Objection: common attributes imply a common notion, contradicting primary diversity.

FrMS88-de3571-d1e177.summary: Reply: the rule is true for non-transcendentals but false for transcendentals, which need not belong to things through any common notion — except perhaps the notion of being, which is in all things, but denominatively in some and quidditatively in others.
claims: Transcendental attributes need not belong to things through a common notion.
Being belongs to some things denominatively and to others quidditatively.

FrMS88-de3571.summary: The eighth question of the prologue asks whether a concept common to simply simple and primarily diverse concepts can be abstracted from them. Meyronnes denies that any common quidditative concept can be abstracted, but identifies four kinds of common concept that can be predicated univocally of them non-quidditatively: second intentions (such as 'ultimate difference' or 'individual property'), the most common attributes (truth and goodness, since all are intelligible and volitable), transcendental relations (identity, diversity, distinction), and privations (unity, simplicity). To the difficulty that an attribute common to many seems to belong to them through a common notion — which would undermine their primary diversity — he replies that this rule holds for non-transcendentals but not for transcendentals, which need not belong to things through any common notion, except perhaps that of being, which belongs to them denominatively rather than quidditatively.
claims: No common quidditative concept can be abstracted from simply simple and primarily diverse concepts.
Second intentions, transcendental attributes, transcendental relations, and privations can be predicated univocally of the primarily diverse.
Transcendental attributes need not inhere through a common notion, unlike non-transcendental attributes.
